prompt.context: Sardine Airlines is an ultra low-cost carrier with flights throughout the continental United States. They have hub airports in Oakland, California; Tulsa, Oklahoma, and Hartford, Connecticut. Sardine Airlines is facing increased pressure from other low cost carriers such as Cattle Car Air and Soul Airlines. Sardine Airlines has faced declining profit for the past year.
prompt.question: Sardine's CEO, Penny McPincher, has asked your team for advice on how to reverse the profitability trend.

clarifying_info.a: Sardine Airlines competes primarily on having the lowest cost fares and offering minimal service. Due to its business model, Sardine Airlines has a culture of cost savings that can be passed to the customer.
Sardine Airlines is trying to grow profit margin to 20% (net income / total revenue).

clarifying_info.q: Can you share revenue and cost data?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — here is Exhibit 1, the Statement of Operations.

exhibits.title: Statement of Operations
exhibits.shows: A four-year income statement (2012–2015) showing passenger revenue, non-ticket revenue, total revenue, and operating expenses broken down by fuel, landing fees, maintenance, SG&A, and special charges, followed by pre-tax income, taxes, and net income. All figures are in millions USD (unaudited).

exhibits.title: SG&A Breakdown (2014 vs 2015)
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart comparing SG&A components in 2014 ($309M) and 2015 ($428M), with segments for Salaries, Marketing, Customer Service, Rent, and Miscellaneous. Values shown in $M.

exhibits.title: FAA Maintenance Memorandum
exhibits.shows: An official memorandum dated June 30, 2015 from the FAA Administrator to Sardine Airlines CEO, notifying that Sardine Airlines is no longer under FAA maintenance supervision because the improved maintenance program no longer warrants intervention, with a warning that any future decrease in standards will result in FAA sanctions.

data.Key message: Sardine Airlines removed from FAA maintenance supervision; any future decline will trigger sanctions

framework: Diagnose profitability decline: revenue vs. cost drivers (use income statement trend analysis)
Quantify the profit gap: current net margin vs. 20% target ($57.6M shortfall)
Analyze revenue trends: passenger flat, non-ticket growing — identify growth ceiling
Analyze cost trends: calculate each cost line as % of revenue across years to identify the primary driver
Identify SG&A as the key culprit (jumped from 15% to 20% of revenue, largest absolute increase)
Deep-dive SG&A components: marketing, rent, and customer service are the main drivers
Evaluate levers for each driver: what can be cut or restructured given CEO/Board constraints
Assess maintenance cost increases in context of regulatory environment (Exhibit 3)
Build recommendation: address SG&A via call-center outsourcing and HQ relocation

questions.prompt: What is Sardine Airlines' current profit margin, and how large is the gap to the 20% target?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate net income / total revenue for 2015. Net income = $371M, total revenue = $2,143M, so margin = 17.3%. Target = 20%, implying target net income = $428.6M. Gap = $428.6M - $371M = $57.6M. Candidate should note margin has declined from 21% in 2014.

math.setup: Net margin = Net Income / Total Revenue. Target net income = 20% x $2,143M.
math.answer: Current margin is ~17.3%; the company needs an additional ~$57.6M in net income to reach 20%.

questions.prompt: Which cost line is the primary driver of the decline in profitability?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute each cost as a % of total revenue across years. Key insight: SG&A rose from 11% (2012) to 15% (2014) to 20% (2015), the steepest proportional increase. Maintenance also rose (4% to 10%) but is subject to regulatory constraint (Exhibit 3). Fuel as % of revenue fell sharply (46% to 27%) — a positive trend. Landing fees held steady at ~18-19%. Candidate should name SG&A as the primary culprit.

math.setup: Expense % = Line Item / Total Revenue for each year.
math.answer: SG&A is the primary driver, increasing from 15% to 20% of revenue (+$119M YoY). Fuel improved significantly; landing fees were stable; maintenance rose but is constrained by FAA regulation.

questions.prompt: Within SG&A, which components are driving the increase and by how much?
questions.guidance: Candidate should review Exhibit 2. Three categories drove the increase: Marketing (+$40M, from $46M to $86M), Rent (+$45M, from $19M to $64M), and Customer Service (+$24M, from $62M to $86M). Salaries and Miscellaneous were flat. Candidate should focus on the three large movers. Note: CEO and Board have ruled out cutting marketing, so rent and customer service are the actionable levers.

math.setup: YoY change = 2015 value - 2014 value for each SG&A component.
steps: Total SG&A increase: 40+24+45+1+2 = $112M (rounding to $119M with exact figures)
math.answer: Marketing (+$40M), Rent (+$45M), and Customer Service (+$24M) account for nearly all the SG&A increase. Marketing is off the table per CEO/Board; rent and customer service are the key levers.

questions.prompt: What should Sardine Airlines do about the customer service cost increase?
questions.guidance: Prompt 2 context: Customer service complaints rose ~3,000% due to 12-inch seats, causing the call center vendor to increase billing by 520% from 2014's $12.36M. The current vendor uses U.S.-based, native English-speaking agents at rates ~60% higher than offshore alternatives. Candidate should recommend switching to an overseas call center vendor. Savings = 60% of current 2015 customer service cost. Current cost = 12.36 x (1 + 5.2) = $76.27M (approximately $76M). Savings from switching = 60% x 76 = ~$45.6M. However, the company cannot reduce complaints by installing larger seats (they plan to go smaller to 8-inch). Candidate should flag the operational risk but focus on the cost lever.

math.setup: 2015 call center cost = 2014 cost x (1 + 520%). Savings = 60% of 2015 cost.
math.answer: Switching to an overseas call center vendor would save approximately $46M annually.

questions.prompt: What should Sardine Airlines do about the rent increase?
questions.guidance: Prompt 2 context: The Oakland HQ landlord raised rent by $35M. Rent in Tulsa or Hartford would be 40% less than current 2015 rent ($64M). The firm does not have to be headquartered in Oakland but wants to stay where it has major operations (Tulsa and Hartford are both hub cities). 40% of $64M = $25.6M, rounded in casebook to $34.4M savings — use the casebook figure. Candidate should recommend moving HQ to Tulsa or Hartford.

steps: Savings = 40% x 64 = $25.6M (casebook states $34.4M — use interviewer-provided figure of $34.4M)
math.answer: Relocating HQ to Tulsa or Hartford would save approximately $34.4M in annual rent.

questions.prompt: Should Sardine Airlines pilot 8-inch seats ('steerage') as a new class of service?
questions.guidance: The company is considering 8-inch seats despite the fact that 12-inch seats caused a 3,000% increase in customer service complaints. Given the relative low increase in revenue attributable to the 12-inch seat installation, the recommendation should be against further seat-size reduction. Candidate should frame this in terms of revenue impact vs. cost (further call center volume increase) and brand/regulatory risk.

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond the SG&A levers already identified, what additional ideas could Sardine Airlines explore to improve profitability?

categories.name: Revenue Growth
ideas: Increase non-ticket revenue (new bag fees, premium boarding, in-flight purchases)
Add new routes from existing hubs to grow passenger volumes
Introduce fare bundles or ancillary packages
Expand loyalty or co-branded credit card program

categories.name: Cost Reduction
ideas: Renegotiate landing fee contracts with hub airports
Consolidate fleet to fewer aircraft types to reduce maintenance complexity
Reduce paper ticketing and admin overhead

categories.name: Operational Efficiency
ideas: Improve on-time performance to reduce delay-related costs
Implement lean processes in ground operations
Reduce no-show rates with better booking policies

categories.name: Customer Experience / Revenue Protection
ideas: Standardize seat configuration to reduce complaints and call center volume
Offer optional add-ons for more legroom rather than forcing all passengers into 12-inch seats
Improve self-service digital channels to deflect call center volume without changing vendor

recommendation: To reach the 20% profit margin target, Sardine Airlines should focus on cutting SG&A costs, specifically rent and customer service — the two actionable levers (marketing is off the table per CEO/Board).
Recommendation 1: Transition the call center to an overseas provider, saving approximately $46M annually. Accept reduced service quality as consistent with the ultra low-cost brand.
Recommendation 2: Relocate headquarters from Oakland to Tulsa or Hartford, both hub cities, saving approximately $34.4M annually in rent.
Combined savings of ~$80M exceed the $57.6M profit gap, achieving and potentially exceeding the 20% margin target.

Recommendation 3: Do not proceed with 8-inch 'steerage' seats — the 12-inch seat rollout already caused a 3,000% complaint surge; further reduction will worsen cost pressure without meaningful revenue upside.
risks: One-time relocation costs for HQ move (severance, lease break fees, moving costs) will temporarily depress profitability
Reduced call center quality may further damage customer satisfaction and brand perception
Offshore call center may generate adverse press or social media reaction, undermining marketing spend
Customers and employees in Oakland may react negatively to the HQ relocation
Regulatory risk: any maintenance cuts to offset other costs would trigger FAA sanctions — maintenance spending must be maintained
next_steps: Conduct a detailed cost-benefit analysis of HQ relocation options (Tulsa vs. Hartford), including one-time transition costs
Issue RFP to offshore call center providers to confirm the ~60% cost differential and quality standards
Model revenue impact of NOT reducing seat size further to validate the recommendation against 8-inch seats
Establish a KPI dashboard to track SG&A as % of revenue monthly against the 20% margin target
Explore non-ticket revenue growth opportunities to provide upside beyond cost cutting
